title: A COLLABORATIVE FRAMEWORK FOR QUANTUM OPTIMISATION AND QUANTUM NEURAL NETWORKS: CREDIT FEATURE SELECTION AND IMAGE CLASSIFICATION
abstract_summary: This preprint presents two case studies applying quantum computing to machine learning: (1) formulating feature selection on the German Credit Dataset as a QUBO and solving it with quantum annealing to produce a two-feature credit-scoring model, and (2) designing Quantum Neural Networks (CRADL and CRAML) with FRQI and compressed FRQI encodings for MNIST digits 3 vs 6 classification. Results show a lightweight credit model with 70% accuracy using two selected features and QNNs that match classical NN performance on the binary digit task, while discussing limitations in hardware scalability and training.
methodology_description: The study addresses two separate tasks. For credit-feature selection the authors reformulate feature selection on the German Credit Dataset as a QUBO (Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization) problem: binary variables indicate feature inclusion, linear terms encode individual feature contributions and quadratic terms encode pairwise interactions. They set penalty/reward coefficients (alpha=0.5, beta=2.0) and a large penalty M=10 to force at least one feature selection. Preprocessing included one-hot encoding of categorical features, standardization of numerical features and a Random Forest importance filter (threshold 0.01) to reduce the initial 832 candidate features. Sub-QUBO extraction heuristics (random selection, influence-value selection, k-opt local search) and a hybrid annealing approach are discussed; the QUBO is solved using quantum annealing / Ising-machine style solvers to obtain a feature subset, and a Logistic Regression model is trained on the selected features and evaluated with precision/recall/F1/support metrics. For image classification (MNIST digits 3 vs 6) they downsample images to 16x16 and 8x8, normalize and binarize pixels, then encode images into quantum states using FRQI and a compressed-FRQI variant to reduce qubit count. Quantum circuit construction uses Hadamard layers on position qubits, controlled-X operations and multi-control gate decompositions (TOFFOLI decomposition into two-qubit gates). Two parameterized QNN architectures (CRADL and CRAML) are proposed: alternating XX and ZZ rotations between pixel, readout and color qubits, with CRAML adding mixed gate operations. Models compared include several QNN configurations and small classical NNs. Training used hinge and MSE losses, an acceleration technique called "mqvector", and 10-fold cross-validation; performance is compared via validation accuracy curves and final accuracy/metrics against classical baselines.
algorithms_used: Gradient-based training (implicit for QNNs and classical NN)
dataset_used: German Credit Dataset (Statlog / UCI): 1000 samples, 20 original features, binary credit-risk label. Also MNIST (handwritten digits); subset for digits 3 and 6 used for image classification.
experiment_input: German Credit Dataset from Statlog/UCI: 1000 samples; preprocessing: categorical features one-hot encoded, numerical features standardized, Random Forest importance filter with threshold 0.01 reducing 832 candidate features to a smaller set. MNIST (digits 3 and 6): training ~12,000 samples, test ~2,000 samples after selecting digits 3 and 6; preprocessing: downsampling to 16x16 and 8x8 (bilinear interpolation), normalization to [0,1] and binarization with threshold 0.5.
experiment_process: Feature selection pipeline: compute RF feature importances -> filter by importance threshold -> formulate QUBO with linear ai and quadratic bij terms and penalties (alpha, beta, M) -> extract sub-QUBO(s) using heuristics (random selection, influence-based, k-opt) -> solve QUBO via quantum annealing / Ising-machine solver -> select features -> train Logistic Regression and evaluate (precision, recall, F1). Image classification pipeline: downsample and binarize MNIST images -> encode images into quantum states using FRQI or compressed FRQI (construct position and color qubits, apply H to position qubits, use controlled-X and controlled rotations with TOFFOLI decompositions) -> build parameterized QNN layers (CRADL/CRAML alternating XX/ZZ gates between pixel/readout/color qubits) -> train models (QNNs and classical NNs) using hinge and MSE loss with mqvector acceleration -> evaluate via validation accuracy curves and 10-fold cross-validation. Key reported hyperparameters: alpha=0.5, beta=2.0, M=10, RF importance threshold=0.01, 10-fold CV. Model configurations reported in paper (resolutions, qubit counts, layers, parameter counts) per Table 3.
experiment_output: For feature selection: selected feature subset ("guarantor" and "residence duration") and downstream Logistic Regression metrics: overall accuracy reported as 70.00%, class-wise precision/recall/F1/support table (Class 0 precision 0.70 recall 1.00 F1 0.82 support 210; Class 1 metrics 0.00 due to model degeneracy). For image classification: validation accuracy curves (hinge and MSE losses), comparative performance between QNN variants (qnn1,qnn2,qnn3) and classical 2-layer NNs (nn1,nn2); qualitative statement that QNNs achieved performance comparable to classical models on 3 vs 6 classification. No detailed confusion matrices or statistical significance tests beyond curves and reported accuracies were provided.
key_findings: [supported] Formulating feature selection on the German Credit Dataset as a QUBO and solving it via quantum annealing produced a two-feature subset ("guarantor" and "residence duration").

[supported] A logistic regression trained on these two selected features achieved 70.00% overall accuracy on the reported test split (with class-wise metrics: Class 0 precision 0.70 recall 1.00 F1 0.82 support 210; Class 1 precision 0.00 recall 0.00 F1 0.00 support 90).
[supported] The QUBO-based pipeline reduced the candidate feature space from 832 potential features (after preprocessing) down to 2 selected features.
[speculative] Whether QUBO-based feature selection is superior to other feature selection methods depends on the dataset (claimed as a general conclusion from their experiments).
[speculative] Quantum annealing efficiently finds the global minimum of QUBO problems by leveraging quantum tunneling (stated as theoretical motivation).

[supported] Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) using FRQI-based encodings (including a compressed FRQI variant) were implemented for MNIST digit (3 vs 6) classification and achieved performance comparable to the classical neural networks studied in the paper.
[supported] Compressed FRQI encoding reduced qubit usage in the QNN experiments without significant observed performance loss (comparison between qnn1 and qnn2 reported).
[supported] QNNs in these experiments exhibited slower initial learning dynamics compared to classical NNs but closed the performance gap over training epochs.

[speculative] The authors attribute improved performance of the CRAML architecture to increased entanglement from mixed XX/ZZ gate layering (the causal mechanism is proposed but not empirically isolated).

[supported] The study identifies practical limitations: current quantum annealers and QNN hardware have limited qubit counts, restricting scalability to larger datasets (e.g., full MNIST), and gradient computation / training for QNNs is computationally expensive relative to classical training.

[speculative] Heuristic sub-QUBO extraction methods (e.g., random selection, influence-based, k-opt) may fail to find global optima for large problems; improving these strategies is proposed as future work.
[speculative] The authors claim the proposed QUBO and QNN frameworks provide a foundation for future quantum-enhanced solutions in finance and computer vision (forward-looking).
results_summary: The preprint reports two case studies: (1) a QUBO-formulated feature selection pipeline solved via quantum annealing on the German Credit Dataset which selected two features (guarantor, residence duration) and yielded a logistic regression with 70% accuracy but poor performance on the minority (high-risk) class; (2) Quantum Neural Network experiments for MNIST digit (3 vs 6) classification using FRQI and a compressed FRQI encoding together with two QNN architectures (CRADL, CRAML), showing that compressed encodings reduce qubit needs and that QNNs can match the classical 2-layer baselines tested after training, albeit with slower initial convergence. The authors discuss scalability and heuristic limitations and propose algorithmic and hardware-focused future work.
performance_claims: 70.00% overall accuracy for logistic regression trained on the two features selected by QUBO (Class 0: precision 0.70, recall 1.00, F1 0.82, support 210; Class 1: precision 0.00, recall 0.00, F1 0.00, support 90).
Feature reduction from 832 potential preprocessed features down to 2 features via the described QUBO pipeline.

Reported QNN model configurations (examples): qnn1 (8×8 input, 6 qubits uncompressed, 12 layers, 72 parameters); qnn2 (8×8 input, 4 compressed qubits, 16 layers, 64 parameters); qnn3 (16×16 input, 6 compressed qubits, 42 layers, 252 parameters).
MNIST 3 vs 6 dataset sizes used: approximately 12,000 training samples and 2,000 test samples for the binary task after preprocessing.
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper reports that quantum methods (QUBO with annealing; QNNs with FRQI encodings) can produce useful solutions on small-scale, toy/benchmarked problems and in some cases match classical baselines, but it does not demonstrate a clear quantum computational or predictive advantage over classical methods; claims of efficiency or superiority are framed as potential or dataset-dependent rather than demonstrated.
limitations: Quantum hardware limitations: current quantum annealers and QNN hardware have limited qubit counts and coupling relationships, restricting scalability to larger datasets (e.g., full MNIST).
Hybrid annealing reliance on heuristics: the hybrid annealing approach depends on heuristic sub-QUBO extraction methods that may not find globally optimal solutions for all datasets.
QNN training cost: gradient calculation for QNNs is computationally expensive, slowing training compared to classical neural networks.

Credit-scoring model limitations: the two-feature model produced poor performance on the high-risk class (Class 1), attributed to small sample size and model simplicity (precision/recall/F1 = 0 for Class 1).
Dataset-dependence of QUBO effectiveness: whether the QUBO method outperforms other feature-selection methods depends on dataset characteristics.
Theoretical weakness of sub-QUBO extraction: existing sub-QUBO extraction methods are heuristic and lack a solid theoretical foundation, limiting guarantees on global optimality.

[inferred] Encoding circuit complexity: the number of gates (and hence circuit complexity) grows exponentially with image size, which may make practical implementation infeasible on near-term quantum hardware despite being tractable in classical simulation.
[inferred] Preprocessing trade-offs: aggressive downsampling and binarization used to reduce qubit requirements may discard important image information and impact generalization.

[inferred] Effects of compression unclear: compressed FRQI reduces qubit usage but the extent of information loss and its impact on more complex datasets or multiclass tasks is not fully characterized.
[inferred] Simulation vs hardware gap: experiments rely on classical simulation accelerations (e.g., mqvector); performance and training dynamics on real noisy quantum hardware remain untested.

[inferred] Limited evaluation scope: experiments focus on binary digit classification (3 vs 6) and a reduced subset of features for credit scoring, so generalizability to broader multiclass problems or diverse financial datasets is uncertain.
[inferred] Error and noise considerations omitted: the paper lacks discussion of noise, decoherence, and error mitigation strategies that are critical for real quantum-device implementations.

key_ideas: #idea:hybrid-approach — Formulate credit-feature selection as a QUBO and solve using quantum-annealer/Ising-style solver combined with classical preprocessing (Random Forest importance filter) and sub-QUBO extraction heuristics to produce a lightweight two-feature credit model.
#idea:hybrid-approach — Use classical Logistic Regression downstream of quantum-selected features (demonstrates a hybrid pipeline: classical preprocessing → quantum optimization → classical model).

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Propose FRQI and a compressed-FRQI encoding plus low-qubit QNN architectures (CRADL/CRAML) to reduce qubit requirements for image classification (MNIST 3 vs 6), aiming at NISQ-era applicability.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Report that QNNs (various small architectures) match classical 2-layer NN performance on the binary digit task, suggesting parity rather than clear quantum advantage on small problems.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Describe practical implementation details (TOFFOLI decompositions, Cirq simulation, mqvector acceleration) and hyperparameters to evaluate trade-offs between resolution, qubit count, layers and parameter count.
contradictions: The paper's empirical findings undermine strong claims of quantum superiority: QNNs only matched (not outperformed) small classical networks on MNIST 3 vs 6, and the QUBO-selected credit model exhibited class-degenerate behavior despite a reported 70% overall accuracy — this contradicts broad claims that quantum approaches will trivially beat classical baselines on such tasks.

Although the work frames compressed encodings and small QNNs as NISQ-feasible, the authors explicitly discuss hardware scalability and training limitations, contradicting optimistic assertions that the presented methods are immediately scalable to real-world financial datasets and QPU deployments.
